items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Ellington’s band play an arrangement, and then have another choice band, maybe like a New York band or an L.A. band, all great musicians, playing the same chart, but the difference, the air that they’re putting in their horns, Carney, Willie Smith, Johnny Hodges, Paul Gonsalves, Jimmy Hamilton

ctx.x: What’s that, I just read a quote from Andre Previn, who said a thousand musicians can get together and play a chord that Stan Kenton wrote and all the arrangers know how to do that. And Duke Ellington writes something for three instruments and they play it and I don’t know what it is.

Well in harmony and in theory it’s really much easier to write for four voices or five voices. But to write for three voices and two voices, because he had three trombone players, and those three trombone players sounded like five or six of them sometimes. But I found after working with the band I discovered in a very short time that you could have Ellington’s band play an arrangement, and then have another choice band, maybe like a New York band or an L.A. band, all great musicians, playing the same chart, but…
Didn’t they play some of your first charts?

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: The Smithsonian has all his manuscripts, so you can see everything is in concert.

I’ve got some of those too. But Duke never like to show people his ideas. He’d show certain people. He showed me how he voiced Caravan. One day he was – on an occasion he was up at the piano, he motioned to me, come here. I got up and sat down by the piano bench. This is Johnny Hodges. [Bellson sings the melody to Caravan.] Up chromatically. Here’s Procope. Here’s Paul [Gonsalves]. You put that all together. The wild thing about Duke’s band is, every individual was a soloist in that band, and yet collectively…

Whew. That was always – their bad night is anybody else’s great night. They never had a bad night. To them they called it a bad night, but it’s really intense. That’s what knocked me out so much. Those five saxophone players sound like ten, not necessarily in volume, but the fullness, the richness that came out of those horns. You had to hear it to appreciate it. I didn’t realize it, listening on record. But seeing it, sitting right next to those guys . . .
